title: Dynamical systems and chaos
audience: a college student in a mathematics degree program (or a related major such as physics, computer science or economics), or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Learn how systems evolve: flows on the line and bifurcations, linear systems in the plane, nonlinear systems, linearization and phase portraits, conservative systems and limit cycles, the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem, Hopf bifurcations, one-dimensional maps and the logistic map, period doubling and chaos, Lyapunov exponents, the Lorenz system and fractal dimension, with simulation in Python.
primary_reading: MIT OpenCourseWare 12.006J Nonlinear Dynamics: Chaos, lecture notes by Daniel Rothman (free online)

weeks.1: Flows on the line and fixed points
weeks.3: Linear systems in the plane and their classification
weeks.4: Nonlinear systems, linearization and phase portraits
weeks.6: Limit cycles and the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem
weeks.8: One-dimensional maps and the logistic map
weeks.9: Period doubling, Feigenbaum scaling and chaos
weeks.11: The Lorenz system and strange attractors

blocks.deliverable: Draw the bifurcation diagram of a supplied one-dimensional system.
Classify the fixed points of a supplied system and sketch its phase portrait.
Prove that a supplied system has a periodic orbit.
Week 7 midterm; locate a Hopf bifurcation and the first period-doubling of the logistic map.
Compute the Lyapunov exponent of the logistic map in code.
Estimate a box-counting dimension from supplied points.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Chaos laboratory: simulate in plain Python the logistic map, a nonlinear oscillator and the Lorenz system, produce a bifurcation diagram, estimate Lyapunov exponents and a fractal dimension with error checks, and write a report that connects each computation to the theorem or definition behind it.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
